title: Jason Cohen on simplifying complex decisions by separating upside from downside
summary: Circular debates happen because pros and cons are mixed together. Jason Cohen says to split upside from downside, decide and invest based on upside, use downside only as a veto, reduce the choice to at most three dimensions, then pick a process and move on.

principles.text: Separate upside from downside to escape circular arguments; each side can be true and the debate still never converges.
principles.quote: The symptom of not following this advice is arguing in logical circles.

principles.text: Decide primarily on upside, and use downside only as a veto when it is unworkable and can't be mitigated.
principles.quote: By basing the primary decision on the upside, and using the downside only as a "veto" when it is unworkable, you have further clarified how to make the decision.

principles.text: Hire leaders for exceptional strengths and fill their weaknesses through the rest of the team.
principles.quote: you should hire based on their exceptional strengths, and then fill in weaknesses using the composition of the rest of the team.

principles.text: Over-invest in a 10x strength rather than lifting weaknesses to neutral; weaknesses are tolerated if the strength is big enough.
principles.quote: developing a 10x strength is far more valuable than shifting a weakness to neutral.

principles.text: Deliberately over-simplify to at most three key dimensions; otherwise you never reach a firm decision.
principles.quote: if you don't intentionally over-simplify, you will never reach a firm and clear decision.

principles.text: Decide quickly with a chosen process; defining the conditions of the decision is most of the work.
principles.quote: Remember that defining the conditions of the decision is 80% of the decision, so invest your time in that.
